top_choice_rationale: The magic-wavelength lattice clock is one separable, measured and independently reproduced achievement: it cancels the light shift while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil broadening, brought uncertainty to about 1e-18, and exposed new many-body physics. Katori (concept, first demonstrations) and Ye (record accuracy, many-body-limited operation) map onto the steps without an arbitrary cut, provided the citation names the lattice clock and not optical timekeeping in general. IceCube is a genuine new window with a secure diffuse flux, but its credit in a large collaboration is representative rather than decisive, so it ranks second; no award is last because a mature, well-attributed achievement exists.
recusal_note: Professional proximity only: atomic physics, laser spectroscopy and precision optics at Lund; Svanberg (doctoral supervisor), Hall's laboratory and the optical-clock community are documented adjacent connections, but no direct tie to Katori or Ye is apparent from the profile.
